interviewQuestions.question: How does a lakehouse table format like Iceberg or Delta Lake achieve ACID transactions on top of plain object storage files?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The mechanism is an added metadata layer that tracks, as a versioned sequence of snapshots, exactly which set of underlying data files constitutes the table at each point in time — with the underlying files themselves staying immutable, plain columnar files on ordinary object storage.

A write operation writes entirely new data files without touching existing ones, and only once every new file is fully and durably written does it attempt to **atomically swap** the metadata layer's current-version pointer to a new snapshot referencing those files. Because that pointer swap is one atomic operation, any reader sees either the complete old snapshot or the complete new one — never a partial mix — and a writer that crashes before the swap simply leaves the pointer unchanged, so readers keep seeing the last valid state with the incomplete files orphaned and harmless.

Concurrent writers are handled with optimistic concurrency control: each writer prepares its change against the snapshot it read, then attempts the pointer swap, which only succeeds if nobody else has already advanced the pointer since that read — a losing writer detects the conflict and retries against the new current state.

The elegant part is that this whole guarantee is built from one primitive — an atomic pointer swap over immutable files — and every other feature (time travel, schema evolution) is really a variation on reading a different snapshot or metadata entry, not a separate mechanism.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the actual mechanism, not just state that these formats 'add ACID to lakes.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: A lakehouse table's query performance has degraded steadily over several months with no code changes. What would you check first?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My first check would be file count and average file size for that table, because a slow, steady degradation with no code change is the signature of small-file accumulation, not a sudden regression. If the table receives frequent small writes — a streaming job committing every 30 seconds, or a micro-batch pipeline — and compaction was never scheduled or has fallen behind, the file count grows continuously while average file size shrinks, and per-file overhead (opening files, reading footer metadata, query planning) increasingly dominates actual data-scan time.

Concretely, I'd look at whether average file size has drifted well below the platform's target range (commonly cited around 128 MB to 1 GB for good performance) — files in the low single-digit megabytes or smaller, accumulating into the tens of thousands, is a strong signal. If so, the fix is running (or properly scheduling) compaction to merge the small files into fewer, larger ones and updating the metadata layer to point at the consolidated set.

If file size looks healthy, I'd check for a second common cause: whether the table's partition or clustering scheme still matches current query patterns — a query pattern that shifted over months without a corresponding change to how the table is organized physically can gradually turn what used to be an efficient predicate-pushdown-friendly scan into something closer to a full scan.

**Testing:** whether you connect a specific symptom (gradual, code-independent degradation) to its most likely mechanical cause rather than treating warehouse/lakehouse slowness as an opaque black box.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide whether to keep a dataset in a plain data lake, or promote it into a lakehouse table format?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd base the decision on whether the dataset actually needs the guarantees a table format adds, since adopting one isn't free — it adds metadata management, requires compaction discipline, and (for time travel) a real storage cost for retained snapshot history.

I'd promote a dataset to a lakehouse table format when: it's updated by more than one writer, or by any writer with retry/failure semantics, where a partial-write inconsistency would actually cause a downstream problem; it needs schema evolution over time in a way that's tracked and enforced rather than discovered by a broken reader; or it benefits meaningfully from time travel — reproducible ML training snapshots, or the ability to roll back a bad write without a separate backup process.

I'd keep something as plain lake files when it's write-once, read-many raw data that's never updated in place (classic bronze-zone raw ingestion, for example) — there's no multi-file atomicity risk if nothing ever gets rewritten, and the extra metadata-layer overhead buys nothing for that access pattern.

A useful rule of thumb: if you'd ever ask 'wait, is this table in a consistent state right now,' or 'can I see what this looked like before that job ran,' that's a strong signal the dataset belongs in a lakehouse table format rather than plain files.

**Testing:** whether you can make a cost-aware adoption decision rather than reflexively recommending the newer, more feature-rich option for everything.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design judgment

interviewQuestions.question: What's the trade-off with optimistic concurrency control in a lakehouse table format, and when would it become a real bottleneck?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Optimistic concurrency control assumes conflicts between concurrent writers are rare, so it lets every writer proceed without locking and only pays a cost — a rejected commit and a retry — when two writers genuinely collide on the same pointer swap. That's a good trade when it holds: for low-to-moderate concurrent writers targeting non-overlapping data (different partitions, different time windows), retry rates stay low and you get full write throughput with no locking overhead at all.

It becomes a real bottleneck when write concurrency climbs and writers increasingly target overlapping data — dozens of writers hitting the same partitions, for instance. Retry rates climb because more attempts collide with a version that's already moved by the time they try to commit, and each retry means re-reading the current snapshot and redoing the metadata preparation, which adds real latency and, at high enough contention, can mean some writers effectively never make progress.

The mitigation is largely architectural, not a config flag: reduce actual write concurrency against the same logical partition (route writes so they don't overlap, batch smaller commits into fewer larger ones), or rely on a table format whose conflict detection is granular enough (partition-level rather than whole-table) that non-overlapping concurrent writers don't collide in the first place even at higher raw concurrency.

**Testing:** whether you understand optimistic concurrency's core assumption and can identify the concrete conditions — high concurrency plus overlapping writes — under which that assumption breaks down.
